sections.heading: What are Math & Number Theory Patterns?
sections.content: Many interview problems can be solved faster by recognizing the mathematics hidden inside them rather than simulating step by step. This topic collects the number-theory tools that appear again and again: GCD and LCM, primes and sieves, factorization, modular arithmetic, fast exponentiation, combinatorics (counting with nCr), digit manipulation, number bases, and careful handling of integer overflow. Each tool replaces a slow brute-force loop with a short formula or an O(log n) or O(sqrt(n)) routine.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Divisibility, remainders, cycles or periodic behavior
GCD, LCM, simplifying fractions or normalizing slopes and ratios
Prime numbers, counting primes, prime factorization, number of divisors
Huge answers that must be returned modulo 1,000,000,007
Large powers (a^b mod m) or inverse of a number modulo a prime
Counting arrangements and paths with combinations (nCr)
Digits of a number: reverse, palindrome, sum of digits, base conversion
Values that overflow Int: factorials, products, sums, powers
Keywords: divisible, prime, gcd, lcm, modulo 10^9 + 7, factorial, power, digits, trailing zeros, number of ways

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Math tricks work because numbers have structure. Every integer is a unique product of primes, so divisibility questions become questions about prime factors. Remainders repeat in cycles, so a huge exponent can be shrunk by working modulo m at every step. Counting problems often have a closed-form answer such as C(n, k) instead of a table. Learning to ask 'is there a formula or a property here?' before coding a simulation is the core skill.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Multiplying two Ints before taking the modulus, which overflows (convert to Long first)
Getting a negative result from % in Kotlin and not adding the modulus back
Computing a^b first and then taking the modulus (use fast exponentiation with mod at every step)
Using Fermat's inverse with a modulus that is not prime
Looping i * i <= n with Int i, which overflows near Int.MAX_VALUE (use i.toLong() * i)
Using Math.sqrt on large values and trusting the floating-point result for exact answers
Math.abs(Int.MIN_VALUE) is still negative, so convert to Long first
Forgetting the edge cases 0, 1, negative numbers and Int.MIN_VALUE
Comparing floating-point slopes or ratios instead of reduced fractions
Starting the sieve inner loop at 2 * i instead of i * i, which is correct but slower

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Look for the math first: a formula, a cycle or a divisibility property often beats simulation
GCD by Euclid runs in O(log n) and is the basis of LCM, fractions and normalized slopes
Use trial division up to sqrt(n) for one number and a sieve for many numbers
Fast exponentiation computes powers in O(log exponent), and with a prime modulus Fermat gives inverses
Always promote to Long before multiplying, and reduce modulo m at every step
Guard digit-manipulation problems against overflow and against Int.MIN_VALUE
